q: Huxley credits whom with founding physical explanations of the body's functions of sustenance and reproduction, via the discovery of blood circulation?
w: René Descartes
Isaac Newton
Charles Darwin
e: Harvey did this for circulation. Huxley says Descartes then did the same for the physiology of motion and sensation.

q: According to Descartes (as quoted by Huxley), the soul doesn't move the limbs directly but determines the course of:
w: The blood in the arteries
Electrical impulses in the nerves
Hormones from the pineal gland
e: The 'animal spirits', a subtle liquid running from the heart through the brain to the muscles. Many movements (heartbeat, digestion, a falling person throwing out their hands) don't depend on the mind at all.

q: Descartes' argument for animal automatism starts from what fact about humans?
w: Humans alone can speak and use language
Humans have immortal and immaterial souls
Humans can reason and do mathematics
e: Reflex actions: we perform coordinated, purposive acts without consciousness or volition. If complex actions can come from mere mechanism in us, why not more complex actions from a more refined mechanism in brutes?

q: Descartes suggests brutes might only simulate intelligence, the way:
w: A parrot simulates a poet
A clock simulates the sun
A mirror simulates a person
e: On this picture brutes are 'a superior race of marionettes' that eat without pleasure and cry without pain.

q: A frog with the front of its brain removed seems blind. Yet when irritated, it jumps around a book placed between it and the light. Huxley concludes:
a: Objects act on its movements without apparent sensation
w: The frog must be secretly conscious after all
The frog has somehow regrown the missing brain
Frogs can sense light through their skin instead
e: Visible objects act through its brain on its motor mechanism without apparent sensation. Complex, precise adaptive behavior (balancing like a rope-dancer) occurs without apparent consciousness.

q: Huxley says Descartes' hypothesis that brutes are unconscious machines:
a: Can't be refuted, but he doesn't accept it
w: Has been decisively refuted by experiment
Is obviously correct and widely accepted
Is incoherent and can't even be stated
e: Can't be positively refuted, but he's not disposed to accept it. He rejects it on the grounds of the doctrine of continuity, not by a knockdown refutation.

q: Because animals lack language, Huxley says they can have no trains of ______, only trains of ______.
w: Feelings; thoughts
Memories; dreams
Desires; beliefs
e: Animals' consciousness 'foreshadows our own', but without language they lack trains of thought.

q: What practical (ethical) reason does Huxley give for erring on the side of treating animals as conscious?
a: The harm to animals if we wrongly assume they can't suffer
w: It's required by Scripture and religious tradition
Animals already have legal rights in most countries
Animals we believe are conscious are more useful to us
e: The terrible consequences for domestic animals if we wrongly assume they can't suffer. He'd be glad if Descartes were right given all the pain in nature, but it's better to err on the right side.

q: Huxley says the brain 'evolves' sensation just as:
a: An iron rod evolves heat when hammered
w: A plant evolves slowly from a seed
A river gradually evolves into a lake
A song evolves from a sequence of notes
e: We have as much right to call sensation an effect of molecular change as to call motion an effect of impact.

q: What does Huxley propose as the physical basis of memory?
w: Animal spirits stored in the heart
Impressions on the immaterial soul
Traces kept in the pineal gland
e: 'Ideagenous molecules': records sensory impressions leave in brain structure. Each impression leaves a brain record that can reproduce a fainter version of the corresponding conscious state.

q: Huxley says an animal's volition (if it has any) is:
a: A sign of physical changes, not their cause
w: The direct cause of its muscular movements
Identical to the state of its brain
An illusion unrelated to the brain
e: An emotion indicative of physical changes, not a cause of them. Like the steam whistle on a locomotive, consciousness is a collateral product with no power over the machinery.

q: Huxley's greyhound example shows that epiphenomenalism is compatible with free will, defined as:
a: Nothing stopping an agent from doing what it wants
w: Acting without any prior cause whatsoever
Choosing to act against one's own desires
Having an immaterial soul that directs action
e: The greyhound chasing a hare is free. Held back by a leash, it isn't, even though it's a machine either way.

q: If animals do have souls, Huxley says the soul relates to the body as:
a: A clock's bell to its works
w: A driver to the car they steer
A captain to the ship they command
Software to the hardware it runs on
e: The bell of a clock to the works, with consciousness as the sound it gives out. Even with a soul, consciousness is an indirect product of material changes in the brain.

q: Applied to humans, Huxley says the feeling of volition is:
a: A symbol of the brain state that causes the act
w: The direct cause of every voluntary act we perform
Proof that humans have an immaterial soul
Something that only humans lack, unlike animals
e: Not the cause of a voluntary act, but a symbol of the brain state that causes it. Our mental conditions are 'simply the symbols in consciousness' of automatic changes in the organism.

q: 'Logical consequences are the scarecrows of fools and the beacons of wise men.' Huxley's point is:
a: Only truth matters, not uncomfortable consequences
w: Logic is an unreliable guide to the truth of things
Wise men should avoid controversial conclusions
A theory's bad consequences prove that it is false
e: The only question is whether a doctrine is true, not whether its consequences are uncomfortable. He anticipates charges of fatalism, materialism and atheism ('the drum ecclesiastic') and says truth comes first.

q: Why does Huxley deny he is a materialist?
a: Matter can't be conceived without a mind
w: He believes in Cartesian immaterial souls
He thinks matter is an illusion from God
He's an eliminativist about the mind
e: He can't conceive of matter existing without a mind in which to picture it. He also denies being a fatalist (necessity is logical, not physical) or an atheist (ultimate causes are beyond reach).
